note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in KS.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Flint Hills National Scenic Byway
byways.designation: Kansas Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-177, Council Grove to Cassoday (about 47 mi); Morris and Chase counties

facts.fact: The byway follows K-177 for 47 miles from US 56 in Council Grove south through Strong City, Cottonwood Falls and Matfield Green to Cassoday.
Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve, established in 1996, protects a remnant of tallgrass prairie, of which less than 4% remains, mostly in the Kansas Flint Hills.
The preserve has kept a bison herd since 2009.
The Chase County Courthouse in Cottonwood Falls was built in 1873 and is the oldest operating courthouse in Kansas.
A travel information radio on 1680 AM, with transmitters at Cassoday, Cottonwood Falls and Council Grove, tells of ranching, pasture burning and prairie wildlife.

byways.review: KDOT designated 1997 (GIS YearDesignated); KDOT name 'Flint Hills National Scenic Byway'.

byways.name: Frontier Military Historic Byway
byways.where: US 69 Alt, US 69, I-435, K-5 and K-7, Oklahoma line near Baxter Springs to Fort Leavenworth (about 168 mi)

facts.fact: The byway runs 168 miles from the Oklahoma border on US 69 Alternate north on US 69, I-435, K-5 and K-7 to the gates of Fort Leavenworth.
It follows a 19th-century trail the Army used to move soldiers and supplies across eastern Kansas, and passes the site of one of the largest cavalry battles of the Civil War.
Fort Scott, now a national historic site, was established in 1842 and its story runs to 1873; the site keeps its parade ground and a patch of tallgrass prairie.
The Battle of Mine Creek was fought on October 25, 1864, in Linn County, where Union cavalry defeated Price's retreating Confederates.
Built in 1827, Fort Leavenworth is the oldest permanent settlement in Kansas.

byways.review: Oldest Kansas byway (KDOT 1990). KDOT GIS line covers only US 69/US 69 Alt, US 54 and K-5 (about 120 mi); the I-435 and K-7 portions are not in the layer.

byways.name: Glacial Hills Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-7 with county roads near Troy, Leavenworth (K-7/K-92) to the Nebraska line at White Cloud (about 63 mi)

facts.fact: The route runs 63 miles north on K-7 from K-92 near the gates of Fort Leavenworth through Atchison and Troy to White Cloud and the Nebraska line, leaving K-7 near Troy for 180th Road, Last Chance Road and 195th Road.
The byway is named for rolling hills and rock-strewn valleys carved by ancient glaciers.
Atchison lies on the Missouri River and was the original eastern terminus of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway.
White Cloud is the seat of government of the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska.

byways.review: KDOT designated 2003. KDOT GIS has about 52 mi (K-7 and US 73); the county-road detour near Troy is not in the layer.

byways.name: Gypsum Hills Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 160, Medicine Lodge to Coldwater (about 42 mi); Barber and Comanche counties

facts.fact: The byway follows US 160 for 42 miles between Medicine Lodge and Coldwater.
The Red Hills, also called Gypsum Hills, owe their color to oxidized iron in Permian red beds, and dissolving gypsum below has left sinkholes across the region.
Kansas Tourism's summary card for the byway (shown on its other byway pages) says buttes, canyons, mesas and sinkholes are rare on the Great Plains but found in the Gypsum Hills.
The Gypsum Hills page describes craggy canyons, red dirt and snow-covered mesas, with wildflowers in spring.
The Medicine Lodge treaties were signed near Medicine Lodge in October 1867 between the United States and southern Plains tribes.

byways.name: Land and Sky Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-27, Sharon Springs (US 40) north through Goodland to the Nebraska line (about 88 mi); Wallace, Sherman and Cheyenne counties

facts.fact: The route runs 88 miles north on K-27 from US 40 in Sharon Springs to the Nebraska state line, with access from I-70 exit 17 at Goodland.
The section of K-27 from US 40 north to Nebraska is designated the Land and Sky Scenic Byway.
Near the north end lie the Arikaree Breaks, loess ravines and gullies on private land reached by back roads.
The Arikaree Breaks are a two-to-three-mile-wide band of badlands carved by water in loess deposits up to 100 feet thick.

byways.review: Not in the catalog. KDOT designated 2016; KDOT GIS RouteDesignationName 'Land and Sky Scenic Byway' (7 features, about 88 mi).

byways.name: Native Stone Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-4, K-99, K-18 and K-177, Dover to I-70 exit 313 near Manhattan via Eskridge, Alma and Wabaunsee (about 75 mi)

facts.fact: The route runs 75 miles from K-4 east of Dover west through Eskridge, north on K-99 to Alma, west on K-18 past Wabaunsee toward Manhattan, and south on K-177 to I-70 exit 313.
Stone barns, roughhewn fences and buildings of locally quarried limestone give the byway its name, and Lake Wabaunsee and a Konza Prairie lookout are interpretive stops.
The Beecher Bible and Rifle Church in Wabaunsee is named for Henry Ward Beecher, who helped smuggle rifles to the town in crates marked Bibles.
Lake Wabaunsee was dug by relief and WPA crews from 1933 and finished in 1937.

byways.review: Designated 2005, extended 2017 (KDOT GIS YearDesignated) east to Dover on K-4 and west to Manhattan and I-70 on K-18/K-177. Catalog line (48 mi) is probably the pre-2017 route.

byways.name: Kansas Pony Express Historic Byway
byways.where: US 36, K-7, K-20, US 73, US 75 and K-148, Troy to the Hollenberg station near Hanover via Horton and Marysville (about 122 mi)

facts.fact: The newest Kansas byway runs 122 miles from US 36 east of Troy by K-7, K-20, US 73 and US 75 through Horton and back to US 36 for about 50 miles to Marysville, then north on K-148 to the Hollenberg Pony Express Station.
The Hollenberg station, built by Gerat H. Hollenberg in 1858 for Oregon and California Trail travelers, is the most intact surviving Pony Express station and a National Historic Landmark.
In Marysville, the Pony Express Home Station No. 1 is a limestone barn of 1859, the only home station still standing on its original site.

byways.review: Not in the catalog. KDOT GIS YearDesignated 2026; RouteDesignationName 'Kansas Pony Express Historic Byway' (11 features, about 124 mi).

byways.name: Post Rock Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-232, Lucas (K-18) to Wilson and I-70 exit 206 (about 18 mi); Russell, Lincoln and Ellsworth counties

facts.fact: The byway follows K-232 for 18 miles from K-18 in Lucas south to Wilson and its World's Largest Czech Egg, and nearly half the route runs beside Wilson Lake.
It is named for Fencepost limestone, which settlers in a treeless country quarried for fence posts and buildings.
K-232 runs along the east side of Wilson Lake and over the top of Wilson Dam.

byways.review: KDOT designated 1998. Catalog line is 16 mi against 18 official; may be short at one end.

byways.name: Prairie Trail Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-156, K-140, K-141, K-4 and McPherson County roads, I-70 exit 225 via Ellsworth, Kanopolis Lake and Lindsborg to Canton (about 80 mi)

facts.fact: The route runs 80 miles from I-70 exit 225 on K-156 to Ellsworth, K-140 and K-141 past Mushroom Rock and Kanopolis state parks, K-4 east to Lindsborg, then Smoky Valley Road to Roxbury and 27th Avenue to Canton.
Mushroom Rock, the smallest Kansas state park, holds concretions of Cretaceous sandstone; the largest rock measures 27 feet across.
Kanopolis State Park has sandstone canyons, yucca and a prairie dog town around Kanopolis Lake.
Lindsborg is known for its Swedish heritage and the biennial Svensk Hyllningsfest.

byways.review: Designated 2007, extended 2015 on McPherson County roads to Canton (KDOT GIS). Catalog line (56 mi) is probably the pre-2015 route.

byways.name: Kansas Historic Route 66 Byway
byways.where: Old US 66 / K-66 / US 69 Alt, Missouri line at Galena via Riverton to the Oklahoma line at Baxter Springs (about 13 mi); Cherokee County

facts.fact: The byway covers Kansas's 13 miles of Route 66 from the Missouri line through Galena and Riverton, over the Marsh Arch Rainbow Bridge, to Baxter Springs and the Oklahoma border.
The Rainbow Bridge over Brush Creek, built in 1923, is the only surviving Marsh arch bridge on the whole length of old US 66 and is on the National Register.
The route passes Nelson's Old Riverton Store, mining-history sites and characters from Pixar's Cars films.

byways.review: KDOT designated 2011. Catalog line is 11 mi against 13 official.

byways.name: Smoky Valley Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 283, K-4 and K-147, a horseshoe from I-70 at WaKeeney to I-70 at Ogallah (about 60 mi); Trego County

facts.fact: The byway is a 60-mile horseshoe from I-70 at WaKeeney south on US 283, east on K-4 and north on K-147 to I-70 at Ogallah.
The Smoky Hills are named for their hazy blue look at sunrise and sunset, and the route loops around Cedar Bluff State Park.
Travelers on the Butterfield Overland Despatch carved their names in Threshing Machine Canyon near Cedar Bluff, and two limestone markers show where the byway crosses the old trail.
Cedar Bluff Reservoir takes its name from juniper-lined limestone bluffs about 100 feet tall.

byways.review: KDOT designated 2003. travelks.com directions say K-177 for the north-south leg; the byway's own page and KDOT GIS show K-147.

byways.name: Western Vistas Historic Byway
byways.where: US 83, K-95 and US 40, Scott City north via Lake Scott State Park to Oakley, then west to Sharon Springs (about 102 mi)

facts.fact: The route runs 102 miles north from Scott City on US 83, through Lake Scott State Park on K-95, past Little Jerusalem Badlands to Oakley, then west on US 40 to Sharon Springs, with a stop at the Fort Wallace post cemetery.
Lake Scott State Park holds El Cuartelejo, the only known pueblo ruin in Kansas, a National Historic Landmark since 1964.
Little Jerusalem Badlands State Park has 220 acres of Smoky Hill Chalk badlands cut into narrow white canyons.

byways.name: Wetlands & Wildlife National Scenic Byway
byways.designation: Kansas Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway
byways.where: K-4, K-156 and Barton, Stafford and Reno county roads, Hoisington via Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira NWR to St. John (about 77 mi)

facts.fact: The 77-mile byway runs from Hoisington east on K-4 past Cheyenne Bottoms, then on K-156 and county roads south past Quivira National Wildlife Refuge to St. John.
The byway joins Cheyenne Bottoms and Quivira, more than 60,000 acres of wetland where millions of migrating birds stop each year, whooping cranes among them.
Cheyenne Bottoms, about 41,000 acres, is the largest wetland in the interior United States.
Quivira's salt marshes are a Ramsar wetland of international importance.

byways.review: KDOT designated 2004. Catalog lists only 'National Scenic Byway'; it is also a Kansas byway.

issues: Land and Sky Scenic Byway (KDOT 2016) and Kansas Pony Express Historic Byway (KDOT GIS year 2026) are not in the catalog; both have KDOT GIS lines (gisValue given).
Native Stone was extended in 2017 and Prairie Trail in 2015 (KDOT GIS YearDesignated); catalog lines (48 and 56 mi) look like the pre-extension routes against 75 and 80 mi official.

travelks.com Smoky Valley directions say K-177 for the north-south leg; KDOT GIS and wakeeney.org show K-147 (K-177 is the Flint Hills highway). Also exit 134 vs 135 at Ogallah differs between the two sites.
Frontier Military KDOT GIS line is about 120 mi and omits the I-435 and K-7 portions; the catalog line (171 mi) is closer to the official 168 mi.

Catalog lists Wetlands and Wildlife only as National Scenic Byway; it is also a Kansas state byway. Catalog names differ slightly from KDOT (e.g. 'Flint Hills Scenic Byway' vs 'Flint Hills National Scenic Byway').

The split between Kansas Tourism (promotion) and KDOT (designation) is inferred from KDOT holding the GIS layer and designation documents; the KDOT document links (dmsweb.ksdot.gov) open in a document viewer and were not read.
Pony Express designation year 2026 comes from the KDOT GIS attribute only; travelks calls it the newest byway.
